sources.entry: Performance Modeling and Design of Computer Systems - Proves why open and closed systems answer a load question differently, and when scheduling, not capacity, sets latency.

summary.title: Performance Modeling and Design of Computer Systems: Queueing Theory in Action
summary.one_liner: A textbook that uses queueing theory, Markov chains and probability to answer computer-systems design and capacity questions, such as open versus closed system behavior and when scheduling policy matters more than capacity.
takeaways: Queueing models can answer what-if questions about server farms, such as whether doubling arrival and service rates keeps mean response time the same.
Little's Law and other operational laws give quick performance relationships without detailed modeling.
Open and closed networks answer load questions differently, and the book explains why.
Heavy-tailed, highly variable job sizes change which scheduling policy (e.g., SRPT, PSJF, FB, PS) performs best.
summary.summary: This is the full table of contents and introduction for Mor Harchol-Balter's 2013 Cambridge University Press textbook on queueing theory for computer scientists. It is organized from probability and Markov chain background through M/M/1 and multi-server queues, queueing networks (Jackson, classed, closed/MVA), and heavy-tailed workloads with phase-type and matrix-analytic methods. The final part covers scheduling in the M/G/1, including FCFS, PS, SJF, SRPT and fairness metrics. The page provides no code or worked material itself beyond the book description and chapter list.
